paragraphs: Event streams contain information both in which events occur and in their timing. This paper introduces a model for learning temporal dependencies in such streams, so that past activity can help explain and predict future events. Its central representation is a conditional event intensity that is piecewise constant: the modeled rate of occurrence stays constant within pieces rather than requiring a continuously changing expression.

The paper provides a closed-form Bayesian method for learning this representation. Forecasting uses a separate importance sampling algorithm, which constructs candidate futures using a proposal distribution based on Poisson superposition. Learning and forecasting therefore have distinct computational roles within the same modeling approach.

Experiments use synthetic data, supercomputer event logs, and web search query logs. These examples illustrate that the learning procedure can efficiently capture nonlinear temporal dependencies and that the sampling procedure can forecast future events effectively. The contribution connects an explicit model of event timing with procedures for both estimating its dependencies and using them for prediction.
neurips-2011-a-model-for-temporal-depend.tldr: A piecewise-constant model learns nonlinear dependencies in event streams and supports forecasting through importance sampling.

paragraphs: Neurons face a mismatch between what they compute and how they communicate: their computations can concern continuously varying quantities, while incoming messages arrive as individual spikes. The paper examines the moment-to-moment fluctuations this creates. It connects two perspectives that are often treated separately: nonlinear processing within dendrites and computation in circuits of spiking neurons.

The central result is that reliably computing even a linear function of incoming signals can require strongly nonlinear components within a neuron's dendritic tree. A simple desired relationship between inputs and output therefore does not necessarily imply simple internal machinery. The nonlinear processing can serve the task of computing reliably when communication itself is pulsatile.

The theory predicts that dendritic nonlinearities and distributions of synaptic weights should match the joint statistics of presynaptic inputs. This gives a computational rationale for some otherwise puzzling dendritic dynamics and plasticity. The claim is conditional: nonlinear subunits can be required for reliable linear computation in this setting, rather than being universally necessary for every neuronal computation.
neurips-2011-active-dendrites-adaptation.tldr: Nonlinear dendritic processing can help neurons reliably compute linear quantities from fluctuating spike inputs.

paragraphs: This paper asks how quickly parallel computation can learn a linear classification boundary when examples have a separating margin. The margin, denoted gamma, matters because the runtime can become much larger as it shrinks. The authors provide both an algorithm that improves this dependence and a limit on parallelizing a familiar alternative.

Their algorithm combines interior point methods from convex optimization with fast parallel matrix computations. Using a number of processors polynomial in the dimension n and in 1/gamma, it runs in approximately O(1/gamma) plus O(log n) time, with the first term stated in soft-O notation. The naive parallel methods considered have at least quadratic dependence on 1/gamma.

The negative result concerns boosting in the original PAC framework, where a booster accesses a weak learner as an oracle. Calling that oracle multiple times simultaneously does not reduce the required number of successive boosting stages. This establishes a specific barrier to parallelizing that oracle-based procedure, while the positive result shows that a different optimization strategy can improve parallel learning time.
neurips-2011-algorithms-and-hardness-res.tldr: An optimization-based parallel learner improves margin-dependent runtime, while oracle-based boosting retains a sequential-stage barrier.

paragraphs: Mini-batch algorithms process groups of examples when updating a model, with the aim of speeding up stochastic optimization. This paper studies that strategy for convex problems. Its question is whether the optimization method itself makes good enough use of mini-batches to deliver the speed-up that motivates using them.

The authors develop an analysis showing that standard gradient methods can sometimes fail to obtain a significant speed-up. They then introduce an accelerated gradient algorithm designed to address this deficiency. The proposed method has a uniformly superior theoretical guarantee in the comparison studied, making the update rule a central part of the argument for better mini-batch performance.

Experiments on real-world datasets support the algorithm and the theoretical insights. The findings connect the way examples are grouped with the way optimization progresses: changing batch organization alone may be insufficient, whereas acceleration can improve the associated guarantee. The theoretical comparison and experimental support are complementary claims; the abstract does not turn them into a claim of faster execution on every possible dataset.
neurips-2011-better-mini-batch-algorithm.tldr: An accelerated gradient algorithm improves mini-batch optimization guarantees where standard gradient methods can offer insufficient speed-up.

paragraphs: Hidden Markov models explain observed sequences through underlying states that are not directly visible. This paper compares two ways to estimate their parameters. Maximum likelihood locally maximizes the likelihood of the observations, while Viterbi training pursues the probability of the most likely hidden-state sequence. Those different objectives can favor different fitted models.

The authors develop an asymptotic analysis using generating functions and apply it to an exactly solvable model containing one unambiguous symbol. In this model, the maximum-likelihood objective has a continuous degeneracy, meaning a continuum of equivalent solutions. The Viterbi objective instead has only finite degeneracy, narrowing the corresponding set of alternatives.

The analysis also finds faster convergence and sparser models for Viterbi training, giving it an automatic preference for simpler explanations in the studied setting. These benefits do not establish universal superiority: in a more general scenario, Viterbi training can perform worse than maximum likelihood while still recovering most parameters correctly. The paper thus explains both an attraction of Viterbi training and a qualification to that attraction.
neurips-2011-comparative-analysis-of-vit.tldr: An asymptotic comparison shows why Viterbi training can favor simpler HMMs, while also identifying settings where maximum likelihood performs better.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing categorization becomes difficult when people are asked to create groups rather than choose from a fixed list of labels. Each annotator may see only part of the collection, use different grouping criteria, and produce a different number of categories. The collection itself may also have categories arranged at several levels of a hierarchy.

The paper proposes a Bayesian model of how annotators approach this clustering task. The model supports inference about both the categories in the data and parameters describing annotators. This treats variation between annotators as part of the inference problem, allowing the method to reason about category structure together with the people supplying the groupings.

Experiments on large image collections suggest that this approach works well and may outperform annotations from a single expert. That is a qualified empirical finding, rather than a guarantee that crowds always produce better categories. The contribution is a framework for assembling partial, differing human categorizations into an inferred clustering while accounting for annotator differences.
neurips-2011-crowdclustering-fa5bed8d60.tldr: A Bayesian model combines partial and differing human groupings to infer categories and annotator characteristics.

paragraphs: Image segmentation assigns categories to pixels, and conditional random fields can express relationships among those assignments. Pixel-level models are large enough that earlier approaches generally used sparse connections. This paper considers the much denser alternative of connecting every pixel to every other pixel, creating graphs with billions of edges.

The central contribution is an efficient approximate inference algorithm for a particular family of these fully connected models. Their pairwise interaction terms must be expressible as linear combinations of Gaussian kernels. That structure makes the dense model computationally usable despite the impracticality of applying traditional inference algorithms to such a large collection of edges.

The experiments show substantial improvements in segmentation and labeling accuracy from dense pixel-level connectivity. The result matters because it makes richer relationships between pixel labels accessible without first reducing the image to a smaller set of regions. The scope remains specific: the algorithm performs approximate inference and relies on the stated Gaussian-kernel form of the pairwise interactions.
neurips-2011-efficient-inference-in-full.tldr: Efficient approximate inference makes fully connected pixel CRFs with Gaussian-kernel interactions practical and improves segmentation in experiments.

paragraphs: Selecting useful variables is difficult when a high-dimensional dataset contains strongly correlated measurements. The paper motivates this problem with genetic and imaging features associated with Alzheimer's disease. Although elastic net addresses correlated-variable selection, the authors identify an opportunity to use the correlation structure embedded in the data more directly.

EigenNet uses data eigenstructures to guide selection within a Bayesian model. It combines a sparse conditional classification component with a generative component that represents correlations among variables. The classification component connects selected variables to prediction, while the generative component brings information about how those variables vary together into the same framework.

The authors develop an efficient active-set algorithm that estimates the model through evidence maximization. Experiments on synthetic and imaging genetics data show better predictive performance than lasso, elastic net, and automatic relevance determination in the comparisons reported. The findings support using the data's correlation structure to guide sparse prediction, with the demonstrated advantage tied to those experiments.
neurips-2011-eigennet-a-bayesian-hybrid-.tldr: EigenNet combines Bayesian classification and correlation modeling to guide sparse variable selection and improve prediction in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Neuronal action potentials commonly appear as brief, sharp voltage spikes, whereas some other action potentials have broad plateaus. This paper asks whether the shape of neuronal spikes can follow from an energy-minimization principle. Its starting assumption is that the brain's need to conserve energy strongly constrains how action potentials are generated.

For a specified spike height, the analysis finds that energy consumption is minimized when the underlying currents follow a bang-bang pattern: they are strong but brief. This produces rapid voltage rises and falls. The result links the visible shape of the spike to an optimization of the currents that generate it.

The same principle predicts additional biophysical features, including very powerful sodium currents that inactivate with voltage, bell-shaped voltage dependence of sodium and potassium kinetics, and cooperative gates that initiate current flow. These properties are not inherently required just to produce a recognizable neuronal spike. Their emergence from energy optimality gives the hypothesis explanatory reach beyond spike shape, while remaining grounded in its stated optimization assumption.
neurips-2011-energetically-optimal-actio.tldr: Assuming energy minimization, the paper derives sharp neuronal spikes and predicts specific properties of their underlying currents.

paragraphs: People appear to combine model-based and model-free reinforcement learning, but the circumstances favoring each approach need explanation. This paper studies how that balance depends on two properties of rewards: noise and volatility. Noise concerns variability in observations, while volatility concerns changes in the reward environment itself.

Through theory and simulation, the authors find that model-free temporal-difference learning is relatively most disadvantaged when volatility is high and noise is low. This is a comparative result about particular environmental statistics. It provides a prediction about when human learners should shift their reliance between learning strategies.

A decision-making experiment manipulates those properties and finds that people change strategies in line with the prediction. The circumstances favoring model-based learning also favor a high learning rate, meaning greater responsiveness to new information. This connection helps explain why psychology has often described the distinction as rule-based versus incremental learning: different strategies can be associated with different speeds of adjustment under the environmental conditions studied.
neurips-2011-environmental-statistics-an.tldr: Theory and a human experiment link shifts toward model-based learning to reward environments with high volatility and low noise.

paragraphs: The task is to label a new dataset using several labeled datasets drawn from similar, but potentially different, distributions. Such variation can arise from biological differences, technical effects, or other sources. The challenge is to transfer what has been learned across related datasets when the new sample has no supplied labels.

The authors develop a distribution-free approach based on kernels. They identify an appropriate reproducing kernel Hilbert space, which supplies the class of prediction functions, and optimize a regularized empirical risk within it. This combines fitting the available labeled examples with a constraint on the learned function's complexity.

The theoretical contributions include a generalization error analysis, descriptions of universal kernels, and a universal consistency result for the methodology. Consistency concerns behavior as data accumulate, rather than promising perfect predictions on a particular finite sample. Experiments on flow cytometry data provide an application of the framework. Together, these contributions give a principled route from several related classification datasets to a new unlabeled collection.
neurips-2011-generalizing-from-several-r.tldr: A kernel-based method transfers classification across related datasets, with generalization analysis and a universal consistency result.

paragraphs: Variational Bayesian matrix factorization approximates uncertainty about two matrices whose product represents the data. A standard approximation treats the two factor matrices as independent. Earlier work showed that adding a stronger independence assumption across columns made the global optimum analytically computable, but it was unclear whether this sacrificed a better solution.

For fully observed data, this paper proves that the global solution under the standard matrix-wise independence assumption already has column-wise independence. The additional restriction therefore does not change the attainable global optimum in this setting. It exposes a property of the optimum rather than imposing a harmful simplification on it.

The practical consequence is that the standard variational problem can be solved analytically and efficiently without iterative algorithms. Experiments illustrate advantages of the analytic solution in probabilistic principal component analysis. The result is specifically about fully observed matrix factorization under the stated variational independence setup; within that scope, it turns an apparently stronger modeling assumption into a justification for direct computation.
neurips-2011-global-solution-of-fully-ob.tldr: For fully observed VBMF, the standard global optimum already has column-wise independence, enabling an efficient analytic solution.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing systems often repeat assignments because individual workers can provide unreliable answers. Repetition improves confidence but also increases cost. This paper formulates the design problem as achieving a target overall reliability while minimizing the number of task assignments, treating that count as the price paid for reliable results.

The authors address both sides of the process: deciding which workers receive which tasks and inferring the correct answers from their responses. These are connected decisions because the information available for answer inference depends on how assignments were distributed. Majority voting supplies a familiar comparison for combining repeated answers.

The proposed algorithm significantly outperforms majority voting and is shown to be asymptotically optimal through comparison with an oracle that knows every worker's reliability. That oracle provides an informed reference point for judging assignment cost. The asymptotic qualification matters: the result describes optimality in the relevant limiting regime, rather than asserting that every finite crowdsourcing instance matches an all-knowing procedure.
neurips-2011-iterative-learning-for-reli.tldr: Joint task-assignment and answer-inference algorithms reduce crowdsourcing cost and achieve asymptotic optimality against a reliability-aware oracle.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to locate a small, relevant group of rows and columns inside a large matrix whose entries are heavily corrupted. The problem is known as biclustering or co-clustering. It arises when relationships between two kinds of entities contain a meaningful subgroup that noise makes difficult to identify.

The authors establish lower bounds on the signal strength needed to recover such a subgroup successfully. Those bounds depend on noise variance, matrix dimensions, and the size of the target bicluster. They also show that a combinatorial procedure using a scan statistic reaches the optimal limit, connecting an impossibility threshold with a procedure that attains it.

The paper separately characterizes the signal-to-noise requirements of computationally tractable methods: entrywise thresholding, thresholding row or column averages, and a convex relaxation of sparse singular vector decomposition. This distinction matters because statistical optimality and computational convenience are different considerations. The results provide a theoretical basis for comparing what these methods require from the data, beyond whether they work on particular examples.
neurips-2011-minimax-localization-of-str.tldr: The paper establishes optimal signal thresholds for noisy bicluster recovery and analyzes the requirements of tractable alternatives.

paragraphs: The problem is to identify the best option in each of several bandit problems, where an option's quality is represented by its mean outcome. Sampling must be allocated across options to make those selections accurately. A central difficulty is distinguishing the best option from competitors whose means are very close.

The authors introduce Gap-based Exploration, or GapE, which focuses on options with small gaps relative to the best mean within their own bandit. A second algorithm, GapE-V, also accounts for outcome variance. The paper proves upper bounds on the probability of making an identification error for both algorithms.

Both methods require tuning an exploration parameter using problem complexity, which is often unknown beforehand. The authors therefore provide variants that estimate this complexity as sampling proceeds. Comparisons with other allocation strategies use synthetic problems. The contribution combines targeted sampling, error guarantees, and a way to address missing prior knowledge about how difficult the identification task will be.
neurips-2011-multi-bandit-best-arm-ident.tldr: Gap-based sampling algorithms identify the best options across multiple bandits, with error bounds and variants that estimate difficulty online.

paragraphs: Ambiguous sensory input can support more than one percept, with perception switching between interpretations. One explanation treats this as probabilistic inference about uncertain input; another emphasizes neuronal adaptation. This paper uses a Deep Boltzmann Machine model of cortical processing to show how both explanations can fit within one framework.

In the model, neuronal adaptation can act as a mechanism that improves sampling-based probabilistic inference. Adaptation therefore has a possible computational role in how the system explores interpretations. This connects a low-level neural mechanism with a higher-level account of what perceptual processing is accomplishing.

The authors analyze switching while the model processes the ambiguous Necker cube, examine the influence of spatial attention, and explore binocular rivalry using the same approach. These investigations offer a model-based perspective on how approximate inference might be implemented in the brain. They support the compatibility of adaptation and probabilistic explanations, without establishing that biological perception necessarily uses a Deep Boltzmann Machine or this particular implementation.
neurips-2011-neuronal-adaptation-for-sam.tldr: A Deep Boltzmann Machine model shows how neuronal adaptation can support probabilistic inference during ambiguous perception.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning starts with an expert's demonstrated actions and tries to infer the reward function behind them. This paper considers that problem in a Markov decision process. Its focus is on learning rewards that can depend nonlinearly on features, extending the common representation as a weighted linear combination.

The proposed probabilistic algorithm uses Gaussian processes to represent the reward function. It also determines how relevant each feature is to the expert's policy. These two elements address different questions together: what shape of reward can explain the behavior, and which supplied features matter for that explanation.

The method allows complex behavior to be captured from demonstrations that are both stochastic and suboptimal. It automatically balances a simpler reward structure against agreement with the observed actions. This matters because demonstrations need not be perfectly consistent or perfectly reward-maximizing to inform learning. The contribution is a probabilistic way to accommodate that behavior while controlling the complexity of the inferred reward.
neurips-2011-nonlinear-inverse-reinforce.tldr: Gaussian processes enable nonlinear reward learning from stochastic, suboptimal demonstrations while assessing feature relevance and balancing complexity.

paragraphs: Some signals need to be separated into a slowly changing positive amplitude envelope and a rapidly oscillating carrier whose instantaneous frequency changes slowly. This decomposition is ill-posed: the observed signal alone does not uniquely determine the desired components. The paper addresses that ambiguity by treating demodulation as probabilistic inference.

The proposed model assigns explicit temporal dynamics to both components. Instantaneous frequency follows an autoregressive extension of the von Mises distribution, while the envelope follows Gaussian autoregressive dynamics subject to positivity. These modeling choices express how the components are expected to evolve over time. A new form of expectation propagation performs inference.

Experiments on synthetic and real signals show that probabilistic amplitude and frequency demodulation outperforms earlier approaches in clean, noisy, and missing-data settings. The stated trade-off is computational demand: the method is expensive despite its demonstrated performance benefits. Its contribution is to make temporal expectations and amplitude constraints explicit parts of the decomposition, giving probabilistic structure to an otherwise ambiguous task.
neurips-2011-probabilistic-amplitude-and.tldr: A probabilistic model separates signal amplitude and frequency effectively across tested data conditions, at substantial computational cost.

paragraphs: Kernel-based reinforcement learning learns a decision policy from sampled transitions and has strong theoretical guarantees. Its practical difficulty is that the model grows with the number of transitions. This paper introduces kernel-based stochastic factorization, or KBSF, to keep the approximator's size fixed while incorporating information from all the data.

The method uses a special factorization of a transition matrix. The resulting algorithm is much faster and still converges to a unique solution. The authors also derive an upper bound on the difference between the value functions computed by the original method and KBSF, giving a theoretical way to assess the approximation.

Experiments cover four reinforcement-learning problems, including learning a neurostimulation policy to suppress seizures in epileptic rat brains. The results demonstrate compression of the original model's information. On the tasks studied, KBSF also outperforms least-squares policy iteration and fitted Q-iteration. These comparisons support its practical effectiveness in those settings alongside the separate convergence and approximation guarantees.
neurips-2011-reinforcement-learning-usin.tldr: Stochastic factorization makes kernel-based reinforcement learning more scalable while retaining convergence and bounding value-function approximation error.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised regression uses both labeled and unlabeled data to learn a prediction function. Many approaches encourage the function to vary smoothly over the data manifold using a graph Laplacian. This paper pursues second-order smoothness, motivated by theoretical work suggesting that it can help achieve faster convergence rates.

The authors connect second-order smoothness to the function's linearity and connect linearity to a parallel gradient field. Their objective therefore balances agreement with observed labels against making the gradient field as parallel as possible. The regularization concerns how the function's changes vary across the manifold, going beyond smoothness of the predictions alone.

The paper first formulates this objective continuously on the manifold, then explains how to discretize it with random points. The resulting optimization is a sparse linear system that can be solved efficiently. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach. Its contribution combines a geometric motivation for the regularizer with a computational formulation that makes the proposed regression procedure practical.
neurips-2011-semi-supervised-regression-.tldr: Parallel-field regularization encourages second-order smoothness in semi-supervised regression and leads to an efficient sparse linear system.

paragraphs: Sparse regularization often expresses preferences about which predictor components are nonzero. This paper develops penalties that can also express preferences about level sets: collections of components whose values exceed a chosen threshold. That expands the structure a regularizer can encode beyond simply selecting a support.

The authors study symmetric submodular functions and their Lovasz extensions. They show that the extension can be understood as the convex envelope of a function depending on level sets. This establishes a route from structural preferences about those sets to convex regularization terms. They also provide optimization methods, including proximal operators, and guarantees concerning permitted level sets and recovery conditions.

Specific choices of submodular function yield a new interpretation of existing norms such as total variation, as well as new norms. Examples use order statistics for clustering and outlier detection, and noisy graph cuts for change-point detection with outliers. The contribution is a unified way to design and optimize penalties around the structure of predictor values.
neurips-2011-shaping-level-sets-with-sub.tldr: Symmetric submodular functions generate convex regularizers that encode structure in predictor level sets, with algorithms and recovery guarantees.

paragraphs: Fitting several structures to data often starts by randomly generating many candidate models and then choosing a subset. The paper identifies a weakness in separating these stages: if sampling misses good candidates, later optimization cannot select them. The quality of the final fit is constrained by the hypotheses already available.

The proposed approach uses reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo to combine hypothesis sampling and optimization. Its hypothesis generator adapts during the process, learning a proposal distribution incrementally and online. Candidate generation can therefore develop alongside the search for a good collection of structures.

The authors prove that the adaptive proposal satisfies diminishing adaptation, a property crucial for ensuring ergodicity in MCMC. This gives theoretical support to changing the proposal while sampling, rather than treating adaptation solely as a computational heuristic. The method is reported to provide superior computational efficiency over other methods. The central contribution is the integration of candidate discovery and model fitting, supported by an analysis of the adaptive mechanism.
neurips-2011-simultaneous-sampling-and-m.tldr: Adaptive reversible jump MCMC combines hypothesis generation with multi-structure fitting and proves diminishing adaptation for its proposal mechanism.

paragraphs: Principal components analysis creates new features by combining the original measurements. Its leading components can be useful for regularizing linear regression, but each may involve every available feature. That makes a component harder to interpret in terms of a small set of original measurements.

This paper develops deterministic and randomized algorithms for constructing sparse eigenfeatures, each involving only a small number of original features. The central guarantee concerns regression performance on the available sample: the constructed features provably achieve performance comparable to regularized linear regression. Sparsity is therefore paired with a direct in-sample performance justification.

The authors describe the algorithms as relatively simple and practically efficient, and demonstrate them on several datasets. Sparse features can improve interpretability and may promote better generalization, but the explicit guarantee stated here concerns in-sample performance. The distinction matters: the work establishes that using fewer measurements per derived feature need not sacrifice comparable training-sample performance, while presenting generalization benefits as a possibility.
neurips-2011-sparse-features-for-pca-lik.tldr: Simple algorithms construct sparse PCA-like features with provable in-sample regression performance comparable to regularized linear regression.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a variational Bayesian inference algorithm for sparse linear models using a spike-and-slab prior. The prior provides a Bayesian basis for selecting a limited set of active contributions. The goal is an inference procedure that can serve several related modeling problems rather than a single application.

The main model combines a common collection of Gaussian process functions using task-specific sparse weights. Tasks can therefore draw on shared functions while using different combinations of them. This construction induces relationships between tasks and supports both multi-task and multiple-kernel learning within the same framework.

The formulation encompasses generalized linear models, sparse factor analysis, and matrix factorization with missing values, allowing the variational algorithm to apply across those cases. Demonstrations cover multi-output Gaussian process regression, multi-class classification, image processing, and collaborative filtering. The contribution is this combination of a sparse Bayesian inference method and a unifying model that makes the method useful across a broad set of learning tasks.
neurips-2011-spike-and-slab-variational-.tldr: A spike-and-slab variational algorithm supports sparse learning across tasks and kernels through shared functions with task-specific weights.

paragraphs: Questionnaires measure unobserved characteristics indirectly through noisy answers. More questions can help estimate those characteristics, but longer surveys can also increase refusal, missing responses, poor-quality answers, and administration costs. This paper studies how to shorten an existing questionnaire while retaining information about the latent variables it was designed to measure.

The authors formulate the task as constrained optimization: choose a subset of a specified size that preserves as much information as possible from an existing latent-variable model. They define an information-theoretic measure to assess the quality of a reduced questionnaire. This makes the selection criterion explicit rather than equating questionnaire quality with its length.

Three approximate inference methods are introduced to address the selection problem, and the paper compares them with a simple but strong heuristic. The optimization target is the best subset of the given size, while the proposed solution methods are approximate. The contribution is a model-based framework for deciding which existing questions retain the most information when survey length must be reduced.
neurips-2011-thinning-measurement-models.tldr: An information-theoretic optimization framework selects shorter questionnaires that preserve information about latent characteristics.
